aiGenerationNote: Produce a 15-minute interactive lab walkthrough. Start by briefly explaining the concept of `systemd` timers, sockets, and path units. Then, guide the user through creating a timer unit and its associated service unit to run a simple script every 30 seconds, showing `systemctl list-timers` and `journalctl` output. Next, demonstrate a path unit: create a directory, set up a path unit to monitor it, and show how creating a file in that directory triggers a service to process it. For the socket unit, explain the concept and show a pre-configured example (e.g., `sshd.socket` if available on the demo system, or a simple custom echo server socket) demonstrating how `systemctl status` indicates listening and how a client connection (e.g., `nc localhost <port>`) would trigger the service. screens.title: Advanced systemd: Timers, Sockets, and Path Units
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore three powerful, event-driven systemd unit types: timers, sockets, and path units. You will learn how timers replace cron by scheduling service activation with precise directives such as OnCalendar and OnUnitActiveSec, and how Persistent can ensure missed runs are executed after a reboot. We’ll see socket units that let systemd accept connections on behalf of a service, launching the daemon only when a client connects and handing off the socket—an efficient way to reduce idle services. Path units use filesystem events, via inotify, to trigger processing when files appear or change. Each unit type is paired with a service unit that defines the work to run. You’ll also learn practical commands for enabling, starting, and verifying these units, plus troubleshooting with systemctl status and journalctl. Together, these tools enable a responsive, resource-conscious system design. By the end of the chapter you will know when to prefer timers, sockets, or path units and how to implement and debug them in real environments.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure and manage systemd timer units to schedule tasks with better integration and logging than cron, implement socket units so services start only when a connection arrives, and set up path units that trigger actions on filesystem events. You will diagnose activation problems using systemctl status and journalctl, and you will make intentional choices about when to prefer timers, sockets, or path units. For example, you’ll configure a timer to run a simple script periodically, enable a path unit to process new files as they arrive, and inspect a socket unit to confirm it is listening and handing sockets to the service. These skills reduce resource usage, improve reliability, and give you stronger debugging signals. You will also learn common pitfalls: forgetting to enable the activating unit, misformatting OnCalendar strings, or omitting daemon-reload after creating new unit files. Mastering these objectives prepares you for real-world administration and for the LFCS exam tasks that involve systemd unit configuration and troubleshooting.

screens.title: Objectives — Practical skills and troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on hands-on execution and the small checks that prevent errors. You will create and enable units, reload systemd, and confirm behavior using list and status commands. For timers, practice choosing between OnCalendar and OnUnitActiveSec and learn when to enable the timer unit versus enabling the service directly. For sockets, verify the ListenStream or ListenDatagram directive and use Accept when the service should fork per connection. For path units, practice PathExistsGlob or PathChanged and configure the paired service as Type=oneshot so it runs and exits. Troubleshooting is part of the objective: you will run daemon-reload after editing unit files, inspect the activated service’s status when socket activation shows listening, and review journalctl entries for error messages. Examples in this chapter include a script that logs a timestamp for timer units and a file processor that renames processed files. These exercises show practical value: less wasted memory, immediate reaction to file arrival, and better logging than cron.

screens.title: What is a systemd timer unit?
screens.narratorSegment: A systemd timer unit is a unit type that schedules the activation of a service unit. Think of the timer as declaring when the work should occur and the paired service as declaring what the work is. Timers are defined in. timer files that contain a [Timer] section with directives such as OnCalendar for calendar-like schedules, OnUnitActiveSec for intervals relative to the last activation, and Persistent which ensures missed runs run after a downtime. Using timers instead of cron offers a few practical benefits: systemd timers integrate with journald for consistent logging, they participate in dependency and target ordering, and they can express dependencies between units. A common mistake is enabling the. service unit instead of the. timer; enabling the timer is what causes scheduled activations. Also remember to run sudo systemctl daemon-reload after creating or editing unit files so systemd notices changes. A concrete example from the lab creates a timer that runs a script every minute using OnUnitActiveSec=60s and logs output to /var/log/timer_output. log. When you configure timers this way, you gain better observability and predictable ordering compared with ad-hoc cron entries.

keyIdea.title: Timer = When, Service = What
keyIdea.text: Define schedule in .timer and the task in .service; enable the .timer to schedule execution.

content.html:
Definition
systemd timer unit
Schedule service activation using .timer files with OnCalendar, OnUnitActiveSec, and Persistent directives.
Key directives
  • OnCalendar — calendar style schedules
  • OnUnitActiveSec — interval since last activation
  • Persistent=true — run missed jobs after boot
Common mistake
Enabling the service instead of the timer prevents scheduled activation; enable the .timer unit.
Key Takeaway

Timers schedule services. Define schedule in .timer and the work in .service, then enable the timer unit.

Example
/usr/local/bin/timer_script.sh
# /usr/local/bin/timer_script.sh
#!/bin/bash
echo "Timer script ran at $(date)" >> /var/log/timer_output.log
/etc/systemd/system/mytimerjob.timer
[Unit]
Description=Run My Periodic Timer Job every minute

[Timer]
OnUnitActiveSec=60s
AccuracySec=1s
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
Commands to activate
sudo systemctl daemon-reload; sudo systemctl start mytimerjob.timer; sudo systemctl enable mytimerjob.timer; systemctl list-timers --all

screens.title: Timer directives and scheduling patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding timer directives helps you choose the right scheduling pattern. OnCalendar accepts calendar-style specifications such as daily, Sun *-*-* 02:30:00, or full timestamps; it is best when you need fixed times or cron-like schedules. OnUnitActiveSec is an interval measured from the service's last activation and is useful for repeating work relative to completion time, like polling or periodic maintenance. AccuracySec controls allowed scheduling jitter to cluster wakeups for power efficiency. Persistent=true is important for reliability: if the system was offline at the scheduled time, a persistent timer will run the missed job at next boot, ensuring delayed maintenance still runs. Remember: enable and start the. timer unit itself; enabling the. service is usually not needed. A frequent troubleshooting step is forgetting sudo systemctl daemon-reload after creating or editing units — systemd will not see new files without reload. Use systemctl list-timers to inspect upcoming events. A misconception is thinking timers replace every cron need; timers integrate better with systemd, but cron remains appropriate for some user-level tasks. Consider dependencies and logging benefits when deciding which to use. Timer directives and scheduling patterns means use oncalendar for fixed times, onunitactivesec for intervals, and persistent for catching missed runs after downtime.. In practical terms, oncalendar, onunitactivesec, persistent, and enabling behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Choose the right directive
keyIdea.text: Use OnCalendar for fixed times, OnUnitActiveSec for intervals, and Persistent for catching missed runs after downtime.

content.html:
Timer directives
Common scheduling patterns
OnCalendar
Calendar-style schedules for fixed times and date patterns. Example: OnCalendar=Sun *-*-* 02:30:00 for Sundays at 02:30.
OnUnitActiveSec
Interval after the unit last became active. Useful for repeating work relative to completion, e.g., OnUnitActiveSec=60s.
Persistent and Accuracy
Persistent=true runs missed jobs after boot. AccuracySec reduces scheduling jitter for efficiency.
Tip: After adding unit files run sudo systemctl daemon-reload. Then enable/start the .timer, not the .service.
Example and verification
Inspect timers
$ systemctl list-timers --all
NEXT                        LEFT  LAST                        PASSED       UNIT                         ACTIVATES
Thu 2026-01-01 03:00:00 UTC  59min Wed 2026-01-01 02:00:00 UTC  1h ago      mytask.timer                 mytask.service
Common troubleshooting
  • Forgot daemon-reload after adding unit files.
  • Enabled the service instead of the timer.
  • Misformatted OnCalendar string causes no schedule.

screens.title: Socket units and socket-based activation
screens.narratorSegment: Socket units enable socket-based activation: systemd opens and listens on a configured socket or FIFO and starts the associated service only when a client connects. This reduces the resource footprint for services that are rarely accessed because the service process does not need to run continuously. The. socket file contains a [Socket] section with directives such as ListenStream for TCP and ListenDatagram for UDP; for example, ListenStream=8080 instructs systemd to listen on TCP port 8080. For services that fork on each connection, set Accept=yes so systemd spawns a new instance per connection. The typical pairing is myservice. socket and myservice. service; you enable and start the. socket unit. When a connection arrives, systemd activates the service and hands the pre-opened socket to it. A common troubleshooting approach is to first confirm that the. socket is active and listening with systemctl status myservice. socket, and then inspect the service unit logs if connections fail to be handled. A frequent misconception is to assume enabling the service is enough: with socket activation you normally enable the. socket to let systemd handle listeners and activation.

keyIdea.title: Socket activation
keyIdea.text: Enable .socket to let systemd accept connections and start the service on demand; use ListenStream and Accept as needed.

content.html:
Definition
systemd socket unit
A .socket unit listens on a socket or FIFO and activates the paired service when a connection arrives.
Listen directives
ListenStream for TCP, ListenDatagram for UDP, specify ports or addresses like ListenStream=8080.
Accept behavior
Accept=yes causes systemd to spawn a new instance of the service per connection; leave Accept=no for single-instance services that receive connections.
Key Takeaway

Socket units let systemd own the socket and start services only when needed, reducing idle resource usage.

Example .socket
[Unit]
Description=My Service Socket

[Socket]
ListenStream=8080

[Install]
WantedBy=sockets.target
Verification
sudo systemctl start myservice.socket; sudo systemctl enable myservice.socket; sudo systemctl status myservice.socket
Troubleshooting tip
If the socket shows active (listening) but the service doesn't handle connections, inspect the service logs with journalctl -u myservice.service to find startup or runtime errors inside the service itself.

screens.title: Path units and filesystem-triggered activation
screens.narratorSegment: Path units are designed to trigger services based on filesystem events. They leverage kernel inotify mechanisms so you can react to new files appearing or to modifications without writing a polling loop. A path unit, for example myprocessor. path, includes a [Path] section with directives such as PathExists, PathExistsGlob, PathChanged, or PathModified. When the condition is met systemd activates the paired service, typically configured as Type=oneshot so it runs a task and exits. An example usage is monitoring a spool directory for incoming files and invoking a processor that renames or moves the file after handling. In the lab we create a directory /var/spool/myincoming, a process_new_file. sh that logs and renames the incoming file, a fileprocessor. service that executes the script with %f so the service receives the triggered filename, and a fileprocessor. path using PathExistsGlob=/var/spool/myincoming/*. If the processor must accept the filename use ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/process_new_file. sh %f and configure the service appropriately. Path units are efficient and reduce complexity compared with custom daemons that poll directories. Path units and filesystem-triggered activation means use path units to react to file events; pair with a oneshot service that receives the filename via %f.. In practical terms, react to file creations and modifications without polling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Efficient filesystem triggers
keyIdea.text: Use Path units to react to file events; pair with a oneshot service that receives the filename via %f.

content.html:
Definition
systemd path unit
Monitor a filesystem path and activate the paired service when conditions are met, using kernel inotify for efficiency.
Common directives
PathExists, PathExistsGlob, PathChanged, PathModified — choose based on the trigger semantics you need.
Service pairing
The service usually uses Type=oneshot and ExecStart with %f to receive the filename that triggered the path unit.
Real example: a processor that logs and renames incoming files, triggered by PathExistsGlob=/var/spool/myincoming/*.
Concrete files
/etc/systemd/system/fileprocessor.path
[Unit]
Description=Monitor /var/spool/myincoming for new files

[Path]
PathExistsGlob=/var/spool/myincoming/*

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
Paired service
[Unit]
Description=File Processor Service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/process_new_file.sh %f
Testing
Create a file in /var/spool/myincoming and watch /var/log/file_processor.log for processing and renaming to .processed.

screens.title: Hands-on: Create a timer job (step-by-step)
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through creating a timer job that runs a simple script every minute. First, create the script at /usr/local/bin/timer_script. sh that appends a timestamp to /var/log/timer_output. log and make it executable. Next, write a service unit mytimerjob. service with Type=oneshot and ExecStart pointing to the script. Then create mytimerjob. timer with OnUnitActiveSec=60s, AccuracySec=1s, and Persistent=true so missed runs execute after reboot. After saving unit files, run sudo systemctl daemon-reload so systemd reads them. Start and enable the timer using sudo systemctl start mytimerjob. timer and sudo systemctl enable mytimerjob. timer. Verify with systemctl status mytimerjob. timer and systemctl list-timers --all. Finally, monitor the log file with tail -f /var/log/timer_output. log to observe periodic entries. A common misconception is expecting the. service to be enabled; the timer handles activation. If you see no entries, confirm daemon-reload, that the timer is active, and check journalctl -u mytimerjob. service for service execution errors. Hands-on: Create a timer job (step-by-step) means create script → service → timer → daemon-reload → start & enable timer → verify logs and status.. In practical terms, script, service unit, timer unit, enable and observe logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Terminal & Unit Files
Timer script

screens.title: Hands-on: Configure a path unit to process new files
screens.narratorSegment: For the path unit lab, begin by creating the monitored directory for incoming files and a small processor script that logs the filename and renames it to indicate processing. Make the script executable and verify permissions so systemd can run it. Next, create fileprocessor. service with Type=oneshot and ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/process_new_file. sh %f; the %f specifier expands to the absolute path of the triggering file. Then define fileprocessor. path with PathExistsGlob=/var/spool/myincoming/* and WantedBy=multi-user. target. After creating the units run sudo systemctl daemon-reload, start and enable the. path unit, and check status with systemctl status fileprocessor. path. To test, create a file in the monitored directory and watch /var/log/file_processor. log for the processor’s log entry and the file being renamed to. processed. Remember a typical misconception: if nothing happens, confirm that the path glob matches the file name and that the service unit’s ExecStart correctly uses %f. Use journalctl -u fileprocessor. service to inspect the processing run and errors. Hands-on: Configure a path unit to process new files means create directory and script → service with %f → path unit with pathexistsglob → daemon-reload → start & enable → test by creating a file.. In practical terms, create directory, processor script, service and path unit then test. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

After creating the units run sudo systemctl daemon-reload, start and enable the. path unit, and check status with systemctl status fileprocessor. path. To test, create a file in the monitored directory and watch /var/log/file_processor. log for the processor’s log entry and the file being renamed to. processed. Use journalctl -u fileprocessor. service to inspect the processing run and errors. keyIdea.title: Path unit steps
keyIdea.text: Create directory and script → service with %f → path unit with PathExistsGlob → daemon-reload → start & enable → test by creating a file.

content.html:
Processor script
# /usr/local/bin/process_new_file.sh
#!/bin/bash
NEW_FILE=$1
if [ -f "$NEW_FILE" ]; then
  echo "$(date): Processing new file: $NEW_FILE" >> /var/log/file_processor.log
  mv "$NEW_FILE" "${NEW_FILE}.processed"
fi
Create directory
sudo mkdir -p /var/spool/myincoming; sudo chown $USER:$USER /var/spool/myincoming
Service and Path unit
fileprocessor.service
[Unit]
Description=File Processor Service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/process_new_file.sh %f
fileprocessor.path
[Unit]
Description=Monitor /var/spool/myincoming for new files

[Path]
PathExistsGlob=/var/spool/myincoming/*

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
Commands to run
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start fileprocessor.path
sudo systemctl enable fileprocessor.path
sudo systemctl status fileprocessor.path
# Test by creating a file
touch /var/spool/myincoming/testfile.txt
sudo tail -f /var/log/file_processor.log

screens.title: When to use timers, sockets, or path units
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between timers, sockets, and path units depends on the triggering event you care about. Use timers when tasks are time-based: scheduled backups, periodic maintenance, or cron replacements where integration with systemd logging and dependencies is beneficial. Timers give you OnCalendar and interval-based scheduling, plus Persistent to handle downtime. Choose socket units when a service can be started on demand as clients connect; socket activation saves memory by avoiding idle daemons and centralizes listening under systemd. It’s ideal for occasional network services or daemons that can accept a pre-opened socket. Pick path units for file-driven workflows: processors that should run when data appears in a directory, log handling, or batch ingestion pipelines. Path units avoid polling by using inotify events. A common misconception is treating these as mutually exclusive: they can be combined — for example, a timer could trigger a sweep while a path unit processes immediate arrivals. Always consider service Type (oneshot vs long-running) and how the activator hands arguments like %f to the service. When to use timers, sockets, or path units means timers for time, sockets for connection events, and path units for filesystem events; mix and match as needed.. In practical terms, select the right activator for your workload. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison
Timer units
Best for scheduled tasks, tight systemd integration and reliable logging.
Socket units
Best for services that can be started on demand when a connection arrives.
Path units
Best for reacting to file appearance or modification without polling.
Practical scenarios
  • Run backups weekly at a certain time — use OnCalendar in a timer unit.
  • Run a web service only when clients connect — use a .socket with ListenStream and Accept if per-connection processes are desired.
  • Process uploaded files as soon as they arrive — use PathExistsGlob to trigger a oneshot processor.
Mixing patterns
You can combine these units. For example, a timer triggers batch cleanup while a path unit handles immediate arrivals. Always match service Type to expected behavior.

screens.title: Diagnosing activation issues
screens.narratorSegment: When timers, sockets, or path units do not behave as expected, a diagnostic pattern makes debugging efficient. First, check the activator: systemctl status myunit. timer, myunit. socket, or myunit. path shows whether systemd recognizes and is running the activator. If the activator is active but the paired service is not performing correctly, inspect systemctl status myunit. service to see failures or start attempts. journalctl -u myunit. service and journalctl -u myunit. timer provide detailed logs recorded by journald, which systemd integrates with for better observability than cron logs. Common mistakes include misformatted OnCalendar values, not running sudo systemctl daemon-reload after adding unit files, enabling the wrong unit (service instead of timer/socket/path), and incorrect service Type for the intended behavior. For path units ensure the glob or path matches the test file; for socket units confirm ListenStream uses the intended port. Use systemctl list-timers and ss or netstat equivalents to confirm listeners when troubleshooting sockets. The key is systematic inspection of activator status, service status, and journal logs. Diagnosing activation issues means check activator status, check service status, review journalctl logs, and confirm daemon-reload and correct unit enabling.. In practical terms, use systemctl and journalctl to find why units fail to activate or run. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.text: Check activator status, check service status, review journalctl logs, and confirm daemon-reload and correct unit enabling.

content.html:
Quick checklist
  1. Confirm unit files exist and are correct
  2. Run sudo systemctl daemon-reload
  3. Start and enable the activator unit (.timer/.socket/.path)
  4. Inspect systemctl status for activator and service
  5. Use journalctl -u <unit> to view logs
Example commands
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl status mytimerjob.timer
sudo systemctl status mytimerjob.service
journalctl -u mytimerjob.service --no-pager
systemctl list-timers --all
sudo systemctl status myservice.socket
journalctl -u myservice.socket
Misconception check
If a socket shows listening but service fails, the problem is likely inside the service’s startup or runtime behavior, not the socket configuration itself.

screens.title: Socket activation demo — how to validate behavior
screens.narratorSegment: In a socket activation demo you validate that systemd listens and that a client connection triggers the service. Start by creating a simple. socket with ListenStream set to a test port and a minimal. service that accepts the socket. After writing unit files, run sudo systemctl daemon-reload and enable/start the. socket. Confirm systemd is listening with sudo systemctl status myservice. socket; the unit should show active (listening). To test activation, use a client such as netcat to connect to the port: nc localhost 8080. The connection causes systemd to start the paired. service and hand the open socket to it. If Accept=yes is set, systemd spawns a new instance per connection. If the service fails to respond, check journalctl -u myservice. service for internal errors. A common error is enabling the. service instead of the. socket; with socket activation you typically enable the. socket so systemd controls the listener. This pattern reduces idle daemons and improves security by minimizing the window a service runs unnecessarily. Socket activation demo — how to validate behavior means enable the .socket, confirm active listenting, and use a client connection to trigger the service; inspect service logs on failure.. In practical terms, enable the .socket, confirm listening, then trigger service start with a client connection. keyIdea.title: Validate sockets
keyIdea.text: Enable the .socket, confirm active listenting, and use a client connection to trigger the service; inspect service logs on failure.

content.html:
Socket unit example
[Unit]
Description=Demo echo service socket

[Socket]
ListenStream=8080

[Install]
WantedBy=sockets.target
Commands
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start demo.service.socket
sudo systemctl enable demo.service.socket
sudo systemctl status demo.service.socket
# Trigger with a client
nc localhost 8080
Observations & checks
  • If the socket is active and listening, systemd accepted the bind.
  • Connecting via nc should start the service; confirm with systemctl status myservice.service.
  • Check journalctl -u myservice.service if the service fails to accept the handed socket or crashes.
Security note
Socket activation reduces the attack surface by keeping the service inactive until needed. Ensure the service has correct privileges before handing it a live socket.

screens.title: Service unit patterns for activators
screens.narratorSegment: When pairing services with timers, sockets, or path units you must choose the correct service configuration. For short tasks triggered by timers or path units use Type=oneshot; these services run a command and exit. For long-running daemons started by sockets use the default Type=forking or Type=simple depending on how the service behaves and whether it expects a pre-opened socket. When using path units that pass a filename to the service, include the %f specifier in ExecStart so systemd substitutes the absolute path of the triggered file. If your service must remain active after handling an event, set RemainAfterExit=no or adjust Type accordingly. Always consider how the activator hands parameters: timers do not pass arguments, sockets hand a pre-opened socket descriptor, and path units can expand specifiers. A common mistake is leaving Type at the wrong value, causing services to be treated as failed or to remain running unexpectedly. As a rule, define the what in the service, keep it focused, and let the activator define when or how it runs. Service unit patterns for activators means use type=oneshot for short triggered tasks, use %f for path-supplied filenames, and pick type based on daemon behavior for sockets.. In practical terms, type, execstart, and specifiers like %f when pairing with activators. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Service patterns
Type=oneshot
Best for timers and path-triggered scripts that run and exit.
Type=simple or forking
Used for network daemons; choose based on whether the process forks or stays in foreground.
Specifiers
Use %f in ExecStart to receive the triggered filename from a path unit.
Example service for path activation
[Unit]
Description=File Processor Service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/process_new_file.sh %f
RemainAfterExit=no
Misconception
Don’t assume the same Type works for all activators. A oneshot for path units and a simple/forking type for socket-activated daemons are common patterns.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore three powerful, event-driven systemd unit types: timers, sockets, and path units. You will learn how timers replace cron by scheduling service activation with precise directives such as OnCalendar and OnUnitActiveSec, and how Persistent can ensure missed runs are executed after a reboot. We’ll see socket units that let systemd accept connections on behalf of a service, launching the daemon only when a client connects and handing off the socket—an efficient way to reduce idle services. Path units use filesystem events, via inotify, to trigger processing when files appear or change. Each unit type is paired with a service unit that defines the work to run. You’ll also learn practical commands for enabling, starting, and verifying these units, plus troubleshooting with systemctl status and journalctl. Together, these tools enable a responsive, resource-conscious system design. By the end of the chapter you will know when to prefer timers, sockets, or path units and how to implement and debug them in real environments.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure and manage systemd timer units to schedule tasks with better integration and logging than cron, implement socket units so services start only when a connection arrives, and set up path units that trigger actions on filesystem events. You will diagnose activation problems using systemctl status and journalctl, and you will make intentional choices about when to prefer timers, sockets, or path units. For example, you’ll configure a timer to run a simple script periodically, enable a path unit to process new files as they arrive, and inspect a socket unit to confirm it is listening and handing sockets to the service. These skills reduce resource usage, improve reliability, and give you stronger debugging signals. You will also learn common pitfalls: forgetting to enable the activating unit, misformatting OnCalendar strings, or omitting daemon-reload after creating new unit files. Mastering these objectives prepares you for real-world administration and for the LFCS exam tasks that involve systemd unit configuration and troubleshooting.

These objectives focus on hands-on execution and the small checks that prevent errors. You will create and enable units, reload systemd, and confirm behavior using list and status commands. For timers, practice choosing between OnCalendar and OnUnitActiveSec and learn when to enable the timer unit versus enabling the service directly. For sockets, verify the ListenStream or ListenDatagram directive and use Accept when the service should fork per connection. For path units, practice PathExistsGlob or PathChanged and configure the paired service as Type=oneshot so it runs and exits. Troubleshooting is part of the objective: you will run daemon-reload after editing unit files, inspect the activated service’s status when socket activation shows listening, and review journalctl entries for error messages. Examples in this chapter include a script that logs a timestamp for timer units and a file processor that renames processed files. These exercises show practical value: less wasted memory, immediate reaction to file arrival, and better logging than cron.

A systemd timer unit is a unit type that schedules the activation of a service unit. Think of the timer as declaring when the work should occur and the paired service as declaring what the work is. Timers are defined in. timer files that contain a [Timer] section with directives such as OnCalendar for calendar-like schedules, OnUnitActiveSec for intervals relative to the last activation, and Persistent which ensures missed runs run after a downtime. Using timers instead of cron offers a few practical benefits: systemd timers integrate with journald for consistent logging, they participate in dependency and target ordering, and they can express dependencies between units. A common mistake is enabling the. service unit instead of the. timer; enabling the timer is what causes scheduled activations. Also remember to run sudo systemctl daemon-reload after creating or editing unit files so systemd notices changes. A concrete example from the lab creates a timer that runs a script every minute using OnUnitActiveSec=60s and logs output to /var/log/timer_output. log. When you configure timers this way, you gain better observability and predictable ordering compared with ad-hoc cron entries.

Understanding timer directives helps you choose the right scheduling pattern. OnCalendar accepts calendar-style specifications such as daily, Sun *-*-* 02:30:00, or full timestamps; it is best when you need fixed times or cron-like schedules. OnUnitActiveSec is an interval measured from the service's last activation and is useful for repeating work relative to completion time, like polling or periodic maintenance. AccuracySec controls allowed scheduling jitter to cluster wakeups for power efficiency. Persistent=true is important for reliability: if the system was offline at the scheduled time, a persistent timer will run the missed job at next boot, ensuring delayed maintenance still runs. Remember: enable and start the. timer unit itself; enabling the. service is usually not needed. A frequent troubleshooting step is forgetting sudo systemctl daemon-reload after creating or editing units — systemd will not see new files without reload. Use systemctl list-timers to inspect upcoming events. A misconception is thinking timers replace every cron need; timers integrate better with systemd, but cron remains appropriate for some user-level tasks. Consider dependencies and logging benefits when deciding which to use. Timer directives and scheduling patterns means use oncalendar for fixed times, onunitactivesec for intervals, and persistent for catching missed runs after downtime.. In practical terms, oncalendar, onunitactivesec, persistent, and enabling behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Socket units enable socket-based activation: systemd opens and listens on a configured socket or FIFO and starts the associated service only when a client connects. This reduces the resource footprint for services that are rarely accessed because the service process does not need to run continuously. The. socket file contains a [Socket] section with directives such as ListenStream for TCP and ListenDatagram for UDP; for example, ListenStream=8080 instructs systemd to listen on TCP port 8080. For services that fork on each connection, set Accept=yes so systemd spawns a new instance per connection. The typical pairing is myservice. socket and myservice. service; you enable and start the. socket unit. When a connection arrives, systemd activates the service and hands the pre-opened socket to it. A common troubleshooting approach is to first confirm that the. socket is active and listening with systemctl status myservice. socket, and then inspect the service unit logs if connections fail to be handled. A frequent misconception is to assume enabling the service is enough: with socket activation you normally enable the. socket to let systemd handle listeners and activation.

Path units are designed to trigger services based on filesystem events. They leverage kernel inotify mechanisms so you can react to new files appearing or to modifications without writing a polling loop. A path unit, for example myprocessor. path, includes a [Path] section with directives such as PathExists, PathExistsGlob, PathChanged, or PathModified. When the condition is met systemd activates the paired service, typically configured as Type=oneshot so it runs a task and exits. An example usage is monitoring a spool directory for incoming files and invoking a processor that renames or moves the file after handling. In the lab we create a directory /var/spool/myincoming, a process_new_file. sh that logs and renames the incoming file, a fileprocessor. service that executes the script with %f so the service receives the triggered filename, and a fileprocessor. path using PathExistsGlob=/var/spool/myincoming/*. If the processor must accept the filename use ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/process_new_file. sh %f and configure the service appropriately. Path units are efficient and reduce complexity compared with custom daemons that poll directories. Path units and filesystem-triggered activation means use path units to react to file events; pair with a oneshot service that receives the filename via %f.. In practical terms, react to file creations and modifications without polling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Choosing between timers, sockets, and path units depends on the triggering event you care about. Use timers when tasks are time-based: scheduled backups, periodic maintenance, or cron replacements where integration with systemd logging and dependencies is beneficial. Timers give you OnCalendar and interval-based scheduling, plus Persistent to handle downtime. Choose socket units when a service can be started on demand as clients connect; socket activation saves memory by avoiding idle daemons and centralizes listening under systemd. It’s ideal for occasional network services or daemons that can accept a pre-opened socket. Pick path units for file-driven workflows: processors that should run when data appears in a directory, log handling, or batch ingestion pipelines. Path units avoid polling by using inotify events. A common misconception is treating these as mutually exclusive: they can be combined — for example, a timer could trigger a sweep while a path unit processes immediate arrivals. Always consider service Type (oneshot vs long-running) and how the activator hands arguments like %f to the service. When pairing services with timers, sockets, or path units you must choose the correct service configuration. For short tasks triggered by timers or path units use Type=oneshot; these services run a command and exit.
